checks.claim: NRC's proposed microreactor framework (May 2026, for reactors of 100 MWe or less) would approve fleets of identical units, allow limited construction ahead of full permitting, and streamline environmental review; NRC's own estimate is $3.76–11.84B in combined savings and licensing-to-deployment in 6–12 months for qualifying designs. It is a proposed rule.
checks.evidence: As of early October 2026, the final rule status remains pending. The proposed rule had a 60-day comment period closing 2026-06-15. State attorneys general filed opposition in June 2026. The rule is expected to issue by the November 23, 2026 deadline set in the May 2026 proposal notice.
checks.correction: NRC's proposed microreactor framework (May 2026, for reactors of 100 MWe or less) proposed fleet approval, construction ahead of full permitting, and streamlined environmental review. As of October 2026, the final rule is pending after a June 2026 comment closure; State AGs filed opposition claiming the fast-track approach violated NEPA.

checks.claim: NRC finalised its risk-informed, technology-inclusive licensing framework in March 2026, the first new reactor-licensing pathway since 1989.
checks.evidence: Part 53 became effective March 13, 2026. It established a risk-informed, technology-inclusive framework for advanced reactors. The rule is in full effect.

checks.claim: The 2024 law directed NRC to produce microreactor-specific licensing strategies across eight areas (done, January 2026) and cut the hourly rate advanced-reactor applicants pay for review from $318 to $148, a concrete cost advantage available now.
checks.evidence: The ADVANCE Act of 2024 reduced the hourly rate for advanced reactor reviews to $148/hour effective in 2025. This rate remains in effect for microreactor and advanced reactor applicants in 2026.

checks.claim: The pilot track produced three critical reactors: Antares' Mark-0 (June 4, at INL), Valar Atomics' Ward 250 (June 18, Utah) and Deployable Energy's 1 MWe Unity (July 1).
checks.evidence: All three Reactor Pilot Program units achieved criticality by the July 4, 2026 deadline as stated. Antares Mark-0 went critical June 4 at INL, Valar Ward 250 on June 18, and Deployable Energy Unity on July 1.

checks.claim: Alaska SB 177 (2022) signed in 2022 with implementing regulations in August 2025.

checks.claim: Section 45Y tax credit provides up to $0.30/kWh for advanced nuclear facilities including microreactors, modified by the Inflation Reduction Act
checks.evidence: Section 45Y provides an investment tax credit (30% of qualifying property costs) and production tax credit (up to $0.30/kWh for 10 years) for advanced nuclear facilities, enacted in 2022 and clarified in 2023-2025 Treasury guidance. Credit remains available for qualifying microreactor projects.

dockets.docket: Utah State Office - proposed land use
dockets.what_it_says: Valar filed a BLM land-use application for a 456-microreactor data center campus in Utah (operation projected 2034+). The filing represents binding commitment of land and water resources, contingent on state trust land lease approval (which Valar announced Sept 17) and NEPA environmental review.
dockets.microreactor_read: First utility-scale microreactor campus filing with a committed buyer (data center) and a concrete site. Defines the regulatory pathway for large co-located generation deployments.

dockets.what_it_says: PJM filed further-compliance tariff amendments in response to FERC's June 18, 2026 binding order in EL25-49, implementing new rules for co-located generation (microreactors paired with data center loads). The filing addresses behind-the-meter generation eligibility and transmission service rules for the region.
dockets.microreactor_read: Co-location in PJM now has defined tariff language and interconnection rights. A data center operator with a microreactor can rely on PJM's published terms rather than negotiating a one-off precedent.

items.headline: FERC rejects Oklo's bid to rejoin PJM interconnection queue
items.what_happened: FERC denied Oklo's request to reinstate its interconnection application at the PJM point in eastern Pennsylvania. Oklo had been accepted in an earlier cluster but Oklo's withdrawal for a withdrawn second site was not eligible for reinstatement under PJM's rules.
items.why_it_matters: A setback for Oklo's Aurora plant path but immaterial to the microreactor buyer landscape; Oklo retains the core PJM interconnection queue and the rejection hinged on Oklo's own filing mistakes, not microreactor-specific barriers. The Aurora site itself is now pursuing DOE authorization rather than NRC licensing.
items.binding_note: FERC order final; the interconnection rejection is binding. It is a negative event for this specific developer but not a policy change affecting the broader market.

items.headline: NRC tells Oklo how it will license a reactor already built under DOE authorization
items.what_happened: NRC issued guidance on how it will license an advanced reactor that was prototype-built and operated under DOE Reactor Pilot Program authorization. Oklo's Aurora (post-prototype) is the first test case, with NRC proposing to treat the DOE data package as the foundation for a streamlined NRC license review.
items.why_it_matters: Establishes a precedent for DOE Reactor Pilot Program graduates: a reactor operated safely at a DOE site can transfer that operational history to NRC licensing, shortening the review cycle relative to a pure paper application. This is material to any microreactor developer planning a DOE-site prototype followed by commercial deployment.
items.binding_note: Guidance only, not a final determination. The actual license application and review process remain pending.

items.headline: State AGs call NRC's microreactor fast-track rule illegal
items.what_happened: 23 state attorneys general filed comments in the NRC Part 57 rulemaking, arguing that the proposed microreactor licensing fast-track violates the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) by streamlining environmental review for fleet approvals without sufficient site-specific analysis.
items.why_it_matters: A legal challenge that delays finalization and may narrow the rule's scope, but it does not block the rule or change the underlying regulatory framework. The challenge is during the comment period; Part 57 is still expected to issue in final form by November 2026.
items.binding_note: The comment filing is binding (it becomes part of the administrative record), but the rule itself is not yet final. The challenge may affect the rule's content but has not yet succeeded in blocking it.

items.headline: U.S. Navy selects Crane, Indiana for its first shore-based microreactor deployment
companies: Naval Surface Warfare Center Crane Division
items.what_happened: The U.S. Navy announced Crane Division in Indiana as the site for its first shore-based microreactor pilot deployment. The selection follows the DOD mandate (10 U.S.C. §2920) to achieve 99.9% energy availability at critical installations by FY2030. No vendor, design, contract terms, or timeline have been disclosed yet.
items.why_it_matters: Opens a concrete military procurement pathway for a microreactor buyer under an explicit statutory mandate. The Crane site is the single highest-profile DoD microreactor anchor, and its selection signals DoD commitment to microreactor procurement and provides a proof-of-concept reference for other installations.
items.binding_note: A site selection announcement only; no vendor contract or procurement timeline has been disclosed. The binding step will be the signed contract award.
